# Counting Requires Distinguishability

R<sup>2</sup>D begins before particles, molecules, forces, fields, energy,
space, time, probability, or information.

It begins with a simpler requirement:

> **Counting requires distinguishability.**

Before something can be measured, modeled, or assigned a physical unit,
there must first be a distinction that can count as one state rather than
another.

If nothing is distinguishable, there is nothing to count.

This is the primitive starting point of Recursively Realized
Distinguishability.

## A Count Is Not Yet a Physical Quantity

Consider the statement:

**There are ten possible realizations.**

The number ten has no units.

It is not ten joules, ten meters, ten seconds, or ten particles. It is a
dimensionless count.

R<sup>2</sup>D begins with these primitive counts and asks how the physical
quantities used by science can later become readable coordinates of their
relations.

This reverses the usual explanatory order.

A conventional scientific description often begins with something like

$$
\text{object}
\rightarrow
\text{physical quantity}
\rightarrow
\text{mathematics}.
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D asks whether the more primitive order is

$$
\text{distinguishable count structure}
\rightarrow
\text{physical read}
\rightarrow
\text{scientific object}.
$$

[Why the mathematics comes before units →](before-units.qmd)

## Boltzmann Provides the Mathematical Clue

The familiar Boltzmann relation is

$$
S = \ln W,
$$

where \(W\) is multiplicity.

R<sup>2</sup>D first reads this not as a statement about thermodynamic
entropy, but as a statement about counting.

Multiplicity \(W\) is the number of distinguishable compatible
realizations belonging to a state.

Equivalently,

$$
W = e^S.
$$

Because \(W\) is a count, it is dimensionless. Its logarithm is therefore
also dimensionless before a later physical calibration is assigned to it.

In Part I, \(S\) is not yet thermodynamic entropy.

It is the logarithmic coordinate of multiplicity.

[Understand multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

## Multiplication Comes Before Logarithmic Addition

Suppose several subordinate distinctions must all be compatible for one
joint realization to occur.

If their multiplicities are

$$
W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_m,
$$

then the number of compatible joint possibilities is

$$
W_{\mathrm{joint}}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{m} W_\alpha.
$$

Taking the logarithm gives

$$
\ln W_{\mathrm{joint}}
=
\sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} \ln W_\alpha.
$$

This is a central mathematical observation in R<sup>2</sup>D:

> **Compatible possibilities multiply. Their logarithmic coordinates add.**

There is a second operation as well.

Within one count domain, mutually exclusive alternatives add.

Thus two very simple count operations sit underneath much of the additive
mathematics later used in science:

- **compatible possibilities multiply;**
- **mutually exclusive alternatives add.**

Logarithms convert multiplicative composition into an additive coordinate.

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore does not reject additive mathematics.

It asks:

> **What is the additive coordinate counting?**

## But Distinguishability Is Not Enough

To say that two things are different is not yet enough to define a scientific
count.

We must also specify **where the distinction is being made**.

Consider a coin.

At one boundary, the readable distinction may be

$$
H \quad \text{or} \quad T.
$$

At another boundary, the object may instead be an ensemble of ten coins,
with readable states such as

$$
(10H,0T),\;(9H,1T),\ldots,(0H,10T).
$$

The individual heads and tails have not simply become blurry.

The count has changed.

What counts as a state at the single-coin boundary is not what counts as a
state at the ten-coin boundary.

This introduces the second primitive requirement:

> **A boundary defines what is being counted.**

[Boundaries define scientific objects →](boundaries.qmd)

## Statistical Mechanics Has No Preferred Object

The same combinatorial structure can describe:

- coins with two readable states;
- molecular switches with two readable states;
- proteins with alternative states;
- spins with alternative states;
- or any other system whose boundary defines the corresponding distinctions.

The mathematics itself does not announce that one of these is the
fundamental object.

The identity of the object comes from the count boundary.

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D does not define *microstate* as "the smallest
thing."

A microstate is a relation to a boundary.

Likewise, a macrostate is not intrinsically "large."

A state can have macrostate meaning at one boundary and microstate meaning
relative to another.

[Macrostate and microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

## The Whole Is Not the Arithmetic Sum of Its Parts

Suppose many subordinate realizations are compatible with the same readable
state.

The enclosing state is not defined by simply adding the subordinate objects
together.

Its multiplicity is the number of compatible subordinate realizations that
the boundary classifies as that state.

Schematically,

$$
\text{subordinate realizations}
\longrightarrow
\text{boundary classification}
\longrightarrow
\text{readable state}.
$$

This distinction becomes fundamental later.

A subordinate transition can change **which realization occurs**.

It cannot, by that transition alone, create the entire multiplicity structure
within which the realization is classified.

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore separates:

> **possible structure**

from

> **particular realization.**

That separation is the beginning of the distinction among multiplicity,
occurrence, and occupancy.

[Multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

[Occupancy and occurrence →](occupancy-occurrence.qmd)

## Counting Changes the Question of Scale

Conventional reasoning often imagines scale change as increased or decreased
resolution of the same underlying object:

$$
\text{same object}
\rightarrow
\text{more detail or less detail}.
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D proposes a different architecture:

$$
\text{change boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change count domain}
\rightarrow
\text{change state meaning}.
$$

Changing scale therefore need not merely hide or reveal detail.

It can change what the scientific object is.

This is the foundation of **recursive replacement**.

[Recursive replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

## The Minimal Example

Coins provide a useful demonstration because they remove nearly all physical
interpretation.

No energy, force, field, temperature, molecular mechanism, or probability is
needed to define the combinatorics.

The example shows how:

1. a boundary defines readable states;
2. subordinate realizations generate multiplicity;
3. realization changes occupancy without creating multiplicity;
4. changing the boundary changes the meaning of the state being counted.

[Work through the coins example →](coins.qmd)

## The Primitive Sequence

The starting architecture can therefore be summarized as

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{state}
\rightarrow
\text{count}
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D then asks what happens when these count domains are recursively
related.

That question leads to macrostate and microstate, multiplicity, recursive
replacement, possibility, constraint, closure, recurrence, and eventually the
R<sup>2</sup>D law.

But the entire structure begins here:

> **Nothing can be counted until something can be distinguished.**
